hints: Think about which plate each beam bends towards, opposite charges attract so match the sign of the particle to the opposite sign on the plate.
walkthrough:
Use attraction to work out the plates**
Picture what you see. The electron beam, which is negatively charged, curves to the left. That can only happen if the left plate is pulling it, so the left plate must be positive. The proton beam, which is positively charged, curves to the right, so the right plate pulling it must be negative.
Final answer: Left plate: positive / + ; Right plate: negative / -

hints: Recall the charge on a neutron and ask yourself whether an electric field can exert a force on a particle with no charge.
walkthrough:
Think about what a field acts on**
An electric field only deflects charged particles. A neutron has no charge, $0$, so there is no electrostatic attraction or repulsion to either plate. Draw the neutron beam going straight up from the source, continuing in the middle without bending to either side.
Final answer: Straight line vertically upwards from the source, undeflected between the plates.

hints: Write out the full electronic configuration of $_{36}\text{Kr}$ up to $4\text{p}$ to see which subshells are occupied.
Remember how many orbitals each subshell type contains, one s orbital holds up to 2 electrons, three p orbitals hold up to 6, five d orbitals hold up to 10.
Count only orbitals that contain at least one electron, for Kr all subshells up to $4\text{p}$ are fully filled.
walkthrough:
Write the full configuration for krypton**
Krypton has atomic number $36$, so $36$ electrons. Filling in order gives $1\text{s}^2 2\text{s}^2 2\text{p}^6 3\text{s}^2 3\text{p}^6 3\text{d}^{10} 4\text{s}^2 4\text{p}^6$. Every subshell listed here is full.

Count s orbitals**
Each s subshell has just $1$ orbital. You have $1\text{s}$, $2\text{s}$, $3\text{s}$ and $4\text{s}$ all occupied, so that is $1+1+1+1 = 4$ s orbitals.

Count p and d orbitals**
Each p subshell has $3$ orbitals. You have $2\text{p}$, $3\text{p}$ and $4\text{p}$ all occupied, so $3+3+3 = 9$ p orbitals. Each d subshell has $5$ orbitals. You have only $3\text{d}$ occupied, and it is full, so $5$ d orbitals.

Final answer: s type: 4 orbitals ($1\text{s}$, $2\text{s}$, $3\text{s}$, $4\text{s}$)
p type: 9 orbitals ($2\text{p}$ x3, $3\text{p}$ x3, $4\text{p}$ x3)
d type: 5 orbitals ($3\text{d}$ x5)

hints: Write the electronic configuration of $_{14}\text{Si}$ and identify which boxes should be empty, half filled or fully filled.
Remember Hund's rule for the $3\text{p}^2$ electrons, they occupy separate orbitals singly with parallel spins before pairing.
walkthrough:
Get the electron count right for silicon**
Silicon is $_{14}\text{Si}$, so $14$ electrons. That gives $1\text{s}^2 2\text{s}^2 2\text{p}^6 3\text{s}^2 3\text{p}^2$. So $4\text{s}$ is completely empty, everything up to $3\text{s}$ is full.

Fill the boxes with correct spins**
Show $1\text{s}$, $2\text{s}$, $3\text{s}$ each as one box with $\uparrow\downarrow$, and $2\text{p}$ as three boxes each with $\uparrow\downarrow$. For $3\text{p}$ you have only $2$ electrons in three boxes, so put one $\uparrow$ in two different boxes and leave the third box empty. The two arrows must point the same way because of Hund's rule, electrons prefer to stay unpaired with parallel spins.

Final answer: $4\text{s}$ empty; $3\text{p}$ has two singly occupied orbitals with parallel spins ($\uparrow$ $\uparrow$) and one empty box; $3\text{s}$, $2\text{p}$ (x3), $2\text{s}$ and $1\text{s}$ all fully filled with paired electrons ($\uparrow\downarrow$).

hints: Identify the orbital shape shown, a figure of eight dumbbell means p, then write the configuration of $_{9}\text{F}$ to count electrons in that subshell type.
walkthrough:
Link shape to electron count**
The dumbbell shape is a p orbital. Fluorine is $_{9}\text{F}$ with configuration $1\text{s}^2 2\text{s}^2 2\text{p}^5$. There are no other p subshells occupied, so the total number of electrons in all orbitals of this p type is $5$.

hints: Identify which electron is removed in every case, a $4\text{s}$ electron, and what two opposing factors control how strongly it is held.
Consider what happens to proton number across Sc to Cu and where the extra electrons are added.
Think about how well $3\text{d}$ electrons shield the outer $4\text{s}$ electron and what this means for effective nuclear attraction.
walkthrough:
Fix on the electron being lost**
In every element from $_{21}\text{Sc}$ to $_{29}\text{Cu}$ the first electron lost comes from $4\text{s}$. So the question is really, why is a $4\text{s}$ electron held with almost the same strength all the way across the row?

Spot the two opposing trends**
Moving across, each step adds one proton, so nuclear charge rises which alone would pull the $4\text{s}$ electron tighter and raise ionisation energy. But the extra electron does not go into $4\text{s}$, it goes into the inner $3\text{d}$ subshell, one shell inside the electron being removed.

See how shielding balances charge**
Electrons in $3\text{d}$ repel and shield the outer $4\text{s}$ electron from the nucleus. The increase in shielding very nearly cancels the increase in nuclear charge, so the net or effective nuclear attraction felt by the $4\text{s}$ electron stays almost constant. Similar attraction means similar energy is needed to remove it.

Final answer: Nuclear charge / proton number increases across Sc to Cu.
Added electrons enter the inner $n=3$ shell / $3\text{d}$ subshell, not the outer shell.
These $3\text{d}$ electrons shield the $4\text{s}$ electron, increased shielding cancels increased nuclear charge so effective attraction on the $4\text{s}$ electron is similar and ionisation energy is similar.

hints: Look at the symbols $^{1}_{1}\text{H}^{+}$, $^{2}_{1}\text{H}^{+}$ and $^{3}_{1}\text{H}^{+}$ and recall what the lower number and upper number tell you about particles in the nucleus.
walkthrough:
Read the isotope symbols**
The lower number is proton number, it is $1$ for all three, so each hydron has $1$ proton in the nucleus. The upper numbers $1$, $2$, $3$ are mass numbers, protons plus neutrons. So neutron numbers are $0$, $1$ and $2$. In short, these are isotopes, same protons, different neutrons.

Final answer: Same: same number of protons (1 proton).
Different: different number of neutrons (0, 1 and 2 respectively).
